🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.06% (intraday, 7-year +15bp). At trading day 18 (last close) it was -1.25% against a five-campaign average of -1.34% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +18bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 710bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +40bp and BB +37bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.32 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Stocks: Nasdaq futures are lower and Dow futures are higher: money is leaving tech for older-economy stocks.
  • FX: The dollar is softer, which lifts the euro and pound; the yen is slightly firmer.
  • Technicals: US stocks sit far above their long-term trend lines, an unusual stretch that often precedes a pullback.
  • Sectors: Over the past week, steady sectors like staples, utilities and energy are beating tech.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most company debt is still priced calmly, but the weakest junk bonds are under real stress.
  • Crisis: No crisis yet, but the riskiest corporate borrowers are getting squeezed. Moderate stress overall.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is cooling slowly, but energy prices and the share of goods rising fast keep it sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations of the whole market look like 2000, but tech earnings multiples are far below that peak.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Bank earnings start with JPMorgan. Equifax has the biggest expected move. US IPOs are quiet this week.
  • Iran: I found no verified reporting for today. The most recent dated report showed US strikes continuing in July.
  • Warsh: Warsh's Fed is holding rates and is hawkish; a hike is possible if inflation doesn't cool.
  • Outlook: Near term: neutral with a defensive tilt. Over the longer run, stretched valuations cap the upside.
  • Trades: Buy 10-year Treasuries, favor staples over tech, and move junk-bond holdings up to safer credits.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 23 hold long, 22 stay out
  • Pre-market: Both watchlists are empty today. Not one of the 12 gappers has a catalyst in the packet, none of them cleared yesterday's high, and the data looks like it's echoing the last session, not a fresh premarket. Sit on your hands until the open gives you real levels.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.56 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 95th pctile, +10bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bank Earnings: 4 banks reported (C, GS, JPM, WFC); no red flags. Credit improving; deposit costs rising.
  • Bottom line: Lower-quality credit is cracking while stocks look calm. Upgrade quality before the rest of the market catches on.

Before the open, money is rotating out of risk and toward quality. Nasdaq futures are down 233.0 points (-0.75%) while Dow futures are up 445.0 (+0.85%) and S&P futures are nearly flat (-6.0). This continues the last session, when the Nasdaq Comp fell 0.44% and the Dow rose 0.38%. Japan led the selling in Asia: the Nikkei fell 1.82% (-1253.4). Europe is mixed: the Euro Stoxx 50 is down 0.37% and the FTSE 100 is up 0.51%. Bonds are rallying across regions. The US 10Y is down about 4bp to 5.1979%, Bunds are 3.446% and Gilts 5.407%, and 10Y note futures are up 0.34375. Oil is easing (Brent 104.79, -1.74%) and the dollar is softer (DXY 102.225). That helps at the margin, but energy is still above $90 WTI. The biggest story under the surface is credit. The headline indexes look calm: US HY OAS is 3.08% (18th percentile) and IG is 0.81% (7th percentile). Inside junk, though, the stress is sharp. Bloomberg's Caa–B gap is 710bp, against a 5-year average near 410bp. It sits in the 99.9th percentile of its 5-year range and is the widest since April 2020. FRED's CCC–B gap is 937bp, the 100th percentile. Is the CCC rot spreading up the ladder? Partly. Single-B OAS widened 40bp over the past month and Ba widened 37bp, so the better-quality junk tiers are repricing too. But the B–Ba gap moved only +3bp and IG only +3bp, so the stress has not yet broken into investment grade. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.52 from 0.27 a month ago, still below its 5-year median of 0.70. The weak tail and the middle of junk are moving together more, but the link is not yet at normal levels. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Sentiment is complacent at the index level: VIX is 15.34 and the S&P and Nasdaq are at 100th-percentile stretch above their trend lines. Positioning is turning defensive at the sector level: staples, energy and utilities are each up more than 4% on the week, while tech is down 1.87%.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

The headline indexes are tight and calm. US IG OAS is 0.81% (z -0.78, 7th percentile, near its historical low of 0.71%) and US HY OAS is 3.08% (z -0.73, 18th percentile). Both show 0 overlap with GFC, EuroDebt and COVID stress levels; HY shows only 6 against the 2022 hike episode. EUR IG is 0.96% (25th percentile), EUR HY 3.45% (30th) and EM USD 1.74% (6th percentile, z -1.25). Beneath the surface, the quality ladder is splitting. The Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 710bp, against a 5-year average around 410bp: 99.9th percentile over 5 years and the widest since 2020-04-24. It widened 77bp in a month and 197bp in 3 months. FRED ICE CCC–B is 937bp (100th percentile) and CCC OAS 1252bp. Contagion into the middle of junk is partial: B is 293bp (+40bp 1m) and Ba is 185bp (+37bp 1m), but the B–Ba gap is just 108bp (+3bp 1m, 34th percentile) and IG is +3bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation rose to 0.52 from 0.27, still below its 0.70 5-year median. B–Ba correlation is 0.86. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Key levels (analyst estimate): HY OAS 3.50% would mean the stress has spread from the CCC tail into broad junk. That would likely need B OAS above about 350bp and the Caa/B correlation back above its 0.70 median. IG at 1.00%+ would need weak bank and financials earnings, with Financials already -3.61% on the month. On the tight side, a return to the 0.71% IG historical low would need Treasuries to keep rallying and the Caa–B gap to stabilize.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.56 vol points (7th percentile of the 41 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.5 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (96bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 12 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 61/100
The answer differs by lens. At the aggregate-market level, today looks like a 2000-style mania. CAPE is about 41 (analyst estimate from cited sources; about 44 at the 1999 peak) and the Buffett indicator is about 236%, above any prior reading. Credit complacency signposts have gone past their 2000-peak conditions: IG tightness is at 132% and Baa–10Y at 166% of peak, VIX complacency at 200%, NFCI looseness at 152%, and commodities-vs-equities at 200% (all computed). The tech-specific froth is much further away. Nasdaq trailing P/E of 42.86 is only 17% of the way to the 175x peak, its stretch versus the 200DMA is 19% of peak, and semis P/E is 55% (computed). The late-cycle catalysts are mixed: the yield curve is 63% and PMIs at 9–10% show no rollover yet. Overall this is a broad valuation and complacency bubble, not a March-2000 tech-earnings mania.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (43x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

On the computed analog chart, the current Nasdaq path from the Oct-2022 low is at month 48, near 248, versus the dot-com path, which ran far higher before peaking at month 113 (1990 anchor) or month 69 (1994 anchor). By time and magnitude, this cycle looks mid-run rather than at the summit. What worries me is the macro and sentiment side. Credit spreads, VIX and financial conditions are all looser than in March 2000, while the CCC tail is already blowing out. In 2000 that combination came before the equity top, not after it. Consumer confidence (17%) and the AAII bull-bear spread (53%) are far from euphoric, so retail mania is not the driver. Margin debt growth of 33.7% YoY (46%) shows leverage building but not at extremes. The top-10 concentration figure is my estimate: sources say the index is as concentrated as it has ever been but give no exact weight. IPO froth is also my estimate: the US calendar is quiet this week while India's is booming.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next meeting (Oct 28): hold, with a hawkish bias (analyst inference). Cited reports put policy at 3.50–3.75% for four straight meetings and Warsh as keeping rates restrictive until inflation recedes. A Monex note judged no change more likely in the coming months even as swaps priced a hike. My search results may lag the latest decision, so I could not verify the current target range.

~1 YEAR

Over roughly a year: a bias to hold or tighten while core PCE is near 3% (3.00759 in the data), with cuts only once the trimmed and median measures hold in the low-2s (analyst inference). The 2Y at 4.7869%, well above the cited policy range, suggests the market prices further tightening. That is my read of the data, not a reported fact.

From his on-record statements as reported: Warsh has warned investors against hunting for rate clues, which points to less forward guidance and more meeting-by-meeting data dependence. He has said there is 'no soft inflation target', a hawkish commitment to 2%. Coverage after his debut meeting said a 2026 hike was now possible, with nine FOMC officials projecting higher rates by year-end. Several of these reports come from lower-tier outlets (cryptobriefing.com), so treat details with caution. The inference that he will lean against cuts despite slowing payrolls (NFP 29.0) is mine.
